Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) has long charged businesses for each worker using its software, a model known as seat-based pricing. The one reason to buy the stock for the next 10 years is that Copilot, its AI assistant, is moving from per-seat subscriptions to usage-based pricing. This could have a significant impact on Microsoft's growth that isn't yet priced into the stock.

The shift to usage-based pricing will allow Microsoft to sell into a bigger market and earn more per customer. The latest numbers in the earnings report show why this is a big deal.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

CEO Satya Nadella said, "The number of Copilot customers actively consuming credits through usage-based billing grew over 75% over the quarter." Customers are increasingly using Copilot to perform higher-value work, driving daily users up fivefold year over year.

Overall, Microsoft's revenue from agents and infrastructure (Azure, 365 cloud, productivity and server licensing, and industry solutions) grew 25% year over year to nearly $77 billion.

Image source: Getty Images.

The momentum in Copilot is a positive signal for investors. It matters because investors have worried that AI would shrink the number of workers Microsoft can charge for, since it can make each worker more productive. But the recent results suggest usage-based offerings can keep revenue growing even when seat counts don't. Microsoft's 365 commercial cloud revenue grew 17% year over year on a reported basis, even though paid seats rose only 5%.

The stock trades at about 27 times forward earnings, and analysts expect earnings to grow about 16% annually over the next several years. That's a reasonable price for a business whose revenue can scale with real work being done with AI over the long term.

Nvidia and Nike are among the latest companies to object to tokenized versions of their shares trading on the ICE-OKX venue, bringing the total to 50, according to Eleanor Terrett.

The venture had initially proposed tokenizing shares from 62 companies.

Objectors include Microsoft, Alphabet, Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan, and the venue's notice gives no reasons for their objections.

A planned venue for trading tokenized U.S. stocks from New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) owner Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) and crypto exchange OKX has hit a wall, as Nvidia (NVDA) and Nike (NKE) joined a growing list of companies objecting to their shares being offered on it.

The number of companies objecting to OKXICE tokenizing their shares has grown to 50, journalist Eleanor Terrett said on X on Sunday. She said Nike, Costco (COST), Micron (MU), Reddit (RDDT) and Nvidia were among the new additions.

See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox

Source: @EleanorTerrett/x

The venture had initially proposed tokenizing shares from 62 companies, Terrett said.

Who's On The List

The venue's notice listed objectors including Microsoft (MSFT), Alphabet (GOOGL), Goldman Sachs (GS), JPMorgan (JPM), Broadcom (AVGO), Verizon (VZ), Intel (INTC) and Walmart (WMT).

AI-linked companies like CoreWeave (CRWV), Oracle (ORCL) and Arm Holdings (ARM) were also on it, along with CrowdStrike (CRWD), Corning (GLW), IREN (IREN) and Bloom Energy (BE). The objections piled up quickly. The venue's October 19 notice showed 16 objectors.

How Would The Venue Work?

OKXICE is a 50-50 joint venture between ICE and OKX, and plans to run under a temporary exemption the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) issued in September, which lets it trade tokenized U.S. stocks without registering as an exchange, according to its public notice.

Trading would run 24 hours a day, seven days a week, with each stock paired against a stablecoin, including such as USDC and Tether's USDT Trades would go through automated liquidity pools on OKX's X Layer blockchain, built on Uniswap (UNI) v4. Only wallets holding a special access token issued by the venue would be able to trade, the notice said.

UNISWAP was one of the top trending tickers on Stocktwits at the time of writing. UNISWAP's price was up by 3% during the past 24 hours. On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment around UNI moved to 'bullish' from 'neutral,' while chatter around it stayed at 'normal' levels over the past day.

Credit: Getty Images

The past two decades have been dominated by digital innovations. From mobile to social to cloud computing and now AI, technology and communication services companies have become the biggest stocks on the planet.

The Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) exchange-traded fund, which comprises the 100 largest nonfinancial stocks on the Nasdaq, has been a great way to play the market's biggest secular growth story of the past 20 years. Just look at this murderers' row of its five biggest holdings: Nvidia (NVDA), Apple (AAPL), Microsoft (MSFT), Micron Technology (MU) and Amazon.com (AMZN), which collectively account for 30% of the ETF.

When it comes to cheap and easy diversification, you can't go wrong with an S&P 500 ETF, such as the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (VOO) or SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY).

Technology and communications names account for almost 48% of the S&P 500, but holding five times the number of stocks versus QQQ means the mega-caps have less influence. Apple, Microsoft and Nvidia represent a significantly larger percentage of QQQ's total assets, amplifying its returns as those specific companies have reached multi-trillion-dollar valuations.

The S&P 500 also holds lots of banking and insurance stocks, which, as noted above, QQQ excludes. The great financial crisis and subsequent era of rock-bottom interest rates did the financial sector — and the S&P 500 — few favors. Financial stocks account for almost 12% of the benchmark index today.

Track all markets on TradingView

The steady ascent of tech and the worst downturn since the 1930s pretty much explain QQQ's extraordinary returns over the past 20 years. To be sure, the S&P 500 has been very good to patient investors, but it lags QQQ by wide margins.

The bottom line on QQQ vs SPY
Credit: YCharts

Have a look at the above chart and you'll see that if you invested $1,000 in QQQ 20 years ago, it would today be worth $20,000. That's good for an annualized total return (price change plus reinvested dividends) of 16.1%.

By comparison, the same sum socked away in SPY would be worth $8,000, or 11% annualized. That's pretty darn good and, importantly, it came with much less volatility.

This last point is key. As they say on Wall Street, there is no such thing as a free lunch. True, QQQ greatly outperformed the broader market, but that outperformance is a risk premium. When the Federal Reserve started rapidly raising interest rates in 2021 and 2022, QQQ fell 36% from its peak. SPY suffered a drawdown of roughly 25%.

Big Tech just had a week investors will remember. At its low on Friday, Alphabet had lost $477 billion in market value for the week, its worst week ever and the second-biggest weekly wipeout for any US-listed stock by Yahoo Finance's calculations, Yahoo Finance reported on October 30.

Most of the damage came Thursday, when the Google parent lost $475 billion in a single session after its third-quarter results. For October as a whole, Yahoo Finance calculated a loss of about $766 billion at Friday's low. That is the second-biggest monthly loss ever for a US-listed company, behind only SpaceX's roughly $822 billion drop in July.

Heavy Losses Spread Beyond Alphabet

Alphabet wasn't alone. SpaceX, Intel and Nvidia each lost more than $100 billion in market value this week, according to Yahoo Finance. Intel fell as much as 30% on Friday after a weak outlook, its steepest drop in decades, and Amazon shed about $70 billion after reporting results Thursday. Software stocks took some of the sharpest hits in percentage terms, with ServiceNow and Fortinet down roughly 25% to 33%.

Nvidia was among the biggest losers. Our analysis of whether Nvidia can sustain its exceptional margins as it becomes more than a chipmaker looks at what keeps its profits so high.

UBS Argues Against Heading for the Exits

Not all the money left the market. Eli Lilly, Tesla and SK Hynix added about $370 billion in combined value over the same stretch, even as the Magnificent Seven stumbled, Yahoo Finance said.

UBS's chief investment office argued against retreating. Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi, the bank's CIO Americas and global head of equities, wrote on Friday that further volatility does not make leaving markets an effective way to protect a portfolio from drawdowns. Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL) made history for all the wrong reasons on Thursday. It shed a staggering $505 billion in market cap after falling 12.6% in the session.

The sell-off was both the largest nominal loss in Alphabet's history and its largest single-session percentage decline.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Alphabet is now out of the $4 trillion club and was just surpassed by Microsoft for the world's third most valuable company behind Apple and Nvidia.

Here's how Alphabet fared during past sell-offs, why a historically powerful valuation metric no longer applies, and what could come next for the communication services stock.

Image source: Alphabet.
Alphabet's FCF yield has plummeted to 0.6%

Buying Alphabet stock today is far riskier than in the past because much of its future earnings growth depends on its artificial intelligence (AI) investments paying off.

Alphabet is investing in the entire AI stack, from its in-house-built Tensor Processing Unit chips (designed by Broadcom) to its frontier Gemini large language models powered by Google DeepMind to Google Cloud infrastructure to AI use cases at the consumer and enterprise application levels. This is a completely different company from the one that last experienced a steep, prolonged downturn.

Let's take a trip back to 2022, when the Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX: ^IXIC) fell by 33.1% -- the worst decline since the index fell 40.5% in 2008. At the worst point, on Nov. 3, 2022, Alphabet closed at a split-adjusted $83.43 per share -- marking a 44.3% drawdown from its all-time high. But the price-to-earnings ratio was just 16.6 -- a dirt cheap valuation for such a high-quality company. And even more importantly, Alphabet's free cash flow (FCF) yield was 5.6%.

Similar to how dividend yield is simply the dividend per share divided by the stock price, FCF yield is the FCF per share divided by the stock price. Like dividend yields, FCF yields increase when a stock's price falls or FCF outpaces the growth rate of the stock price. A FCF yield of 5.6% is incredibly strong -- meaning that if Alphabet wanted to, it could theoretically support a 5.6% dividend purely on FCF. Or use that cash to buy back stock, reinvest in the business, or bet big on its best ideas without harming its balance sheet.

Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) posted results for the fiscal first quarter of 2027 (the three months ending Sept. 30, 2026) on Wednesday, Oct. 28. Revenue climbed 19% year over year to $92.3 billion, and earnings per share grew 18% on a non-GAAP (adjusted) basis.

The stock hardly moved. Shares trade near $530 as I write, about 2% under the record close of $543.45 they set on Oct. 13.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

This quiet response makes sense to me. The quarter combined great growth in Microsoft's cloud business with another big jump in spending. I graded the report on the three things I think matter most to shareholders today: Azure's growth against the company's own forecast, spending and margins, and the outlook.

Image source: The Motley Fool.

1. Azure beat Microsoft's forecast

I give Azure an A.

In early September, Microsoft narrowed what it counts as revenue from Azure, its cloud computing platform, and changed its forecast to match. The forecast was for Azure revenue growth of 44% to 45% in constant currency in the fiscal first quarter. Azure instead grew 48%. And it did that even though some third-party data center capacity Microsoft expected in the quarter was late.

Showing how high demand for the platform still is, Azure's growth has sped up sharply over the last year. Under the new definition, it grew 40% a year ago, 42% in the fiscal fourth quarter (the period that ended in June), then 48% in the September quarter. In other words, Azure is growing faster today than it was a year ago, even after passing $100 billion in revenue in fiscal 2026.

"Customer demand continues to exceed available supply," CFO Amy Hood said on the company's fiscal first-quarter earnings call.

Earlier this month, I wrote that I thought Microsoft shares needed Azure to keep growing faster than 40%. It cleared that bar easily.

2. Cash flow took a hit

I'd give spending and margins a C+.

Capital expenditures came to $45.2 billion in the fiscal first quarter. This compares to $34.9 billion a year ago (up around 30%) and $41 billion in the fiscal fourth quarter. Of course, the total could have been higher had the delayed capacity arrived on time.

The spending is hurting free cash flow. Cash flow from operations climbed 29% year over year to $58 billion. But free cash flow dropped around 27% to $18.6 billion, down from $25.7 billion a year earlier and $19.6 billion in the fiscal fourth quarter.

Yes, Microsoft's operating margin inched up to 50%, from 49% a year ago. But Microsoft Cloud's gross margin dipped to 66%, from 68% a year earlier, because lower-margin Azure made up a bigger part of cloud sales.

The money is going into capacity that customers already want. Still, free cash flow shrinking while profits grow isn't a trend I can grade far higher.

3. Azure should speed up again

The outlook gets a B+.

For the fiscal second quarter, management forecast revenue between $96 billion and $97.1 billion, or growth of 18% to 19%, around the same rate as the fiscal first quarter. More importantly, management expects Azure revenue to climb 49% to 50% in constant currency.

But management also expects operating margins to dip slightly year over year. And it sees Windows OEM and devices revenue dropping in the mid-30% range, partly because of lower PC demand and a year-ago quarter that got a boost from the end of Windows 10 support. Plus, capital expenditures should pass $50 billion in the fiscal second quarter, taking spending in calendar 2026 to around $170 billion.

I'd still call it a strong outlook, as Azure is arguably the figure that matters most for the stock.

Is Microsoft stock a buy now?

Overall, the report gets an A, a C+, and a B+, which is better than I thought going in.

In the past four reported quarters, Microsoft's adjusted earnings per share totaled about $18.04. With the stock around $530, shares cost about 29 times adjusted earnings. Before the report, the stock cost about 31 times adjusted earnings.

Last weekend, I wrote that I'd want to buy the stock closer to $465. The Azure grade is what moves me. With growth well above my 40% bar, I'm less worried the stock might deserve a lower price-to-earnings multiple than I used. And because my buy price is linked to adjusted earnings, a quarter like this raises it.

But the spending grade stops me from paying $530. With free cash flow shrinking, I think 29 times adjusted earnings already reflects most of the good news. I'm closer to buying than I was a week ago. But I'd still want a lower price.

Nvidia has been one of the biggest winners of the AI boom, but its stock has cooled off as investors fret that Big Tech is overspending on data centers. The shares climbed more than 1,200% over the past three calendar years, yet they're up only about 13% so far in 2026.

The stock has at least held up better than most. When AI and chip stocks lost more than $1 trillion in combined value during one week in mid-October, Nvidia fared better than many of its peers. Now one of its biggest customers has offered a fresh reason for optimism. Microsoft's latest report showed where its AI money is going, and much of it is landing on chips.

Microsoft's spending tilts heavily toward chips

Microsoft reported its fiscal first-quarter results on October 28, posting revenue of $92.3 billion, up 19% from a year earlier, while its Azure cloud business grew 48%, according to Microsoft. Net income rose 32% to $36.6 billion. Strong cloud demand like that is exactly what keeps chip orders flowing.

Also read: Nvidia has a stake in SpaceX that came from an unexpected place

The detail that matters most for Nvidia came in the spending breakdown. Roughly three-quarters of Microsoft's $45.2 billion in quarterly capex went toward "short-lived assets," a group that includes CPUs, GPUs, and data center networking gear. That works out to roughly $34 billion in a single quarter, much of it on the kind of hardware Nvidia sells.

Microsoft isn't easing off, either. The company expects capex to top $50 billion in the second quarter and has guided for about $170 billion in calendar-year spending, with the increase driven by CPUs and GPUs. It also said it expects to remain cash-flow positive.

Microsoft is spending because customers keep asking for more. Capex, including finance leases, actually came in a bit below analyst forecasts, yet the company guided for Azure growth of 49% to 50% next quarter and said Copilot users jumped 50% from the prior quarter, SiliconANGLE reported. "We still have demand that exceeds supply," chief financial officer Amy Hood said.

Why this matters so much for Nvidia

Nvidia leans heavily on customers like Microsoft. In its fiscal second quarter, Nvidia's revenue more than doubled to $96.2 billion, and its data center business brought in $89 billion of that, up 117% from a year earlier, according to Nvidia. That means data centers account for about 92% of total sales. Net income rose 126% to $59.7 billion.

That concentration cuts both ways. Strong cloud spending can send Nvidia's results soaring, but any pullback by the biggest buyers would hit it hard. That's why investors pore over every capex update from Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta.
